title: A Punnett Square Predicts the Chances

scenes.visual: Two Pp parents; predicted chances graphic, about 3 purple : 1 white, labelled not a drawn sample; question appears.
scenes.tts: Two pea plants both have purple flowers. Both carry one purple allele and one white allele. Most of their offspring, their young plants, are predicted to bloom purple. About one in four is predicted to bloom white. Where was the white hiding? Could we predict it before planting a single seed?

scenes.visual: Body cell with two gene copies that become a P bar and a p bar; dominant and recessive rules; p stays in the cell.
scenes.tts: Each body cell of a pea plant carries two copies of the flower color gene. An allele is one version of a gene. Pea plants have a purple allele and a white allele. Scientists write them as capital P and small p. A dominant allele shows with only one copy. A recessive allele shows only with both copies. The small p is hidden, not destroyed.

scenes.visual: Table of PP, Pp, pp with flower colours; a Pp plant splits into a P sex cell and a p sex cell, 50 percent each.
scenes.tts: The pair of alleles a plant carries is its genotype. The trait that shows is its phenotype. Two purple alleles, or one of each, look purple. Only two white alleles look white. Each sex cell carries one allele. A plant with one of each passes on either allele, with a fifty percent chance each.

scenes.visual: A 2 by 2 grid; P and p across the top and down the side; the four boxes fill in; each box 1 in 4.
scenes.tts: A Punnett square is a grid of every way two parents' sex cells can join. Write one parent's sex cells across the top, and the other's down the side. Fill each box with its two letters. Each box has a one in four chance.

scenes.visual: The filled square is coloured by phenotype; ratio 3 purple : 1 white; the pp box traced to a p from each parent; 1 in 4 = 25 percent.
scenes.tts: Read the boxes. One has two purple alleles, two have one of each, and one has two white alleles. A ratio compares two numbers: three purple to one white. Probability is the chance something will happen. White needs both parents to pass on the white allele. That chance is one in four, or twenty-five percent.

scenes.visual: Four purple offspring, 32 percent; Mendel's seed-shape bars 5,474 and 1,850 with a 3 to 1 line; the answer.
scenes.tts: The square gives the chance for each offspring, not an exact count. Four seeds from two parents with one of each might all bloom purple. The chance of that is about thirty-two percent. Mendel counted thousands of pea seeds. His seed shape counts came out about two point nine six to one, close to three to one but not exact. So we can predict the chances, and real counts land near them.
